utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. I believe Mr. Morrissey has something to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do. Sorry, pardon me, Your Honour. I do have something to raise. We don't have any proofing notes for Mr. Karavelic, and we got a list last night of 50 exhibits that the Prosecution wants to tender through that person or wants to use with that person. Now, the result of all of that is that, in my submission, we wouldn't be in a position to agree to starting that witness at all today, even in evidence in chief. We have to be in a position to object to documents if we see fit. We have to get instructions from the accused man about the proofing notes. We don't know whether they're extensive or not. I'm sorry. I regret doing this. I think it's important to make a bona fide effort to speed things along as best as possible, but the time has now been reached where I just have to say in discharging my job as an -- attempting to be competent counsel, I couldn't agree to it at the moment. I'm sorry to take that position, but that's where I find myself now. So that's what I have to say at this stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner. I'm extremely sorry to hear that the proofing notes have not been furnished to the Defence at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I spoke with Mr. Re. They proofed the witness to 7.30 last night. They completed the proofing notes last night. They're four and a half pages. First thing this morning they brought the witness in. He read -- they've had translated the proofing notes to him. He's made corrections. The corrections are being typed. We should have them within five minutes. They were just finalising the corrections and bringing him to a signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, on our list we have many witnesses. I must say, four witnesses before the summer -- before the recess, sorry. And it seems to me it's not realistic for us to finish all those witnesses before the recess. However, the problem for us is we could not allow a witness to testify in a half way and wait for two weeks and a half and come back to continue. We don't know what would happen during this two and a half weeks. And we also believe that it is not fair to start a witness if the Defence has not got the proofing notes yet. So what shall we do? Yes, Mr. Morrissey. Do you have any good suggestions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do have, I hope, Your Honour. In my submission, the appropriate course is not to proceed with the witness Delalic next week. We can proceed with this witness once we've got the proofing notes, once we've had time to get instructions. We can do that today. Your Honours may or may not know this, but we can't visit on weekends at the UNDU. We're not -- we just can't. Sometimes it can be arranged to do so late on a Friday, but even that causes major headaches. But in any event, we -- what would be -- one way to handle it is we could spend -- finish the witness that's here now. That's important because she's six months pregnant. And then spend the rest of the day in dealing with the proofing notes which I'm told we'll get in five minutes, and we can get -- we may be able to get access to Mr. Halilovic today. We'll do everything we can to arrange that. We also have to get -- okay. Sorry, I'm making a speech. I'll stop that. So that's the best way to proceed in my submission. We can start that witness on Monday when the witness Adie finishes. And I think it's fair to say that we would finish that witness within the week, and if there was any danger of it, we could tell the court and extra sittings might be able to be arranged. But my view is that we would be able to finish that witness. And I think we may also be able to finish the pathologist. There is no chance, however, that we would finish Ramiz Delalic next week, none. So that seems to be the only way we can viably proceed. Can I indicate that if we had Karavelic -- sorry, Mr. Karavelic, I think that the pathologist -- there is going to be some cross-examination with the pathologist and a bit more than there was with the last one because at Grabovica there's no dispute at least there were some -- she didn't have much to say, and in any event we're not disputing that there were obviously some killings that took place there. But things are a bit more complicated at Uzdol, of course But having said that, it may be that the Prosecutor wants to lead 89(F) evidence in relation to that. We can talk to them about that. And the cross-examination is, I think, under control. So that's my view. I think we can accomplish everyone except for the witness Delalic next week. Obviously there's -- there are two others that we don't know about at the moment; that's Mr. Alispahic and of course Mr. Mujezinovic. But I understood that the Prosecutors weren't going to call them next week in any event, or weren't proposing to, so we to go into -- into -- the Prosecution case will go over the break anyway; in other words, there was no chance of finishing it. So that's my suggestion, Your Honour. The Prosecutors will have something to say about it. I have got a couple of other matters to raise about -- other matters to raise but I think if we're talk about scheduling now, perhaps I'll just keep those, and we can talk about those a little bit later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would suggest that we get the proofing notes and we start the witness Karavelic today, this afternoon. However, if the Court's not taking that view, would rather start him on Monday, I would agree the best thing we do is we start with Kate Adie on Monday, finish her, then go into Karavelic and then try to finish off the pathologist at the end of the week. We would not have a chance to do Ramiz Delalic. We will just have to bring him back after the break, the two-week break, and we the can proceed with the final three or four witnesses that exists, that are remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the only problem is that whether we are going to sit this afternoon or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, my submission is not, frankly. Experience shows that if the Defence -- the better prepared the Defence is the shorter the cross-examination is, and really we need that time. I frankly indicate that when we get the proofing notes because Mr. Karavelic is rather like Mr. Cikotic, a person who may have some expertise to bring to bear, but we don't know yet but he might have. As with Mr. Cikotic we might seek to -- we might ask to speak to him ourselves. We haven't decided that yet, and it's not appropriate to do it until we get the proofing notes. It's not even appropriate to ask to do so yet. We just want to see the proofing notes before we make any such decision. Then we'll ask and then we'll see what response we get. But Your Honour, really we -- I think in good conscience I have to say we cannot proceed this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I just want to make one quick comment. The remark was the better prepared the Defence is the shorter the cross-examination. With or without the proofing notes, cross-examination will not start until probably Tuesday, if not Wednesday. So either with or without the proofing notes, they're going to have them this morning, in the best situation cross-examination won't start until mid-Tuesday or Wednesday, so they still have four days to work on the matter, to prepare for cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we still don't want to start this afternoon. We have to take instructions. We have to be in a position to object to certain documents, and at the moment we still don't even have the proofing notes, frankly, so we're just not ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm extremely sorry about this situation, and the -- it seems to me that it is not fair, at least to the Defence team, that we'll start the witness without the proofing notes. In the meantime, the Defence needs some time to discuss with their client concerning this, with all the documents furnished to the Defence, which I heard there are a lot of documents that will go through this witness. So we decided to continue the present witness and finish her as early as possible and let her go back for the weekend, because she's in a very delicate condition. We cannot keep her for very long. We are not going to sit this afternoon to give enough time to the Defence to prepare for their case. Next Monday, we'll hear Ms. Kate Adie, and we'll try to finish her in one day. Right after that we'll hear Karavelic and to see how far we have to go. But, however, we at least have to finish Karavelic next week. This is the most safer approach at this moment. It is so decided. Well, Mr. Morrissey, as for the other matters, are you going to talk it now or after we finish the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had in mind after we finished the witnesses, and in fact I haven't even brought the list with me. If I could just be excused briefly to fetch it I will, but I think the witness is here, and I had in mind she should be finished as quickly as possible and then I an raise some matters. I didn't have in mind to ask Your Honours to make any quick rulings on the spot today. There's just some matters that now we're coming towards the end of the Prosecution case we need to determine, the Karic issue, the record of interview issue, and there are a number those sort of issues of that been flagged in the past, and we just need to know in some cases what the Prosecution's position about those is, so it would be appropriate to raise them at the end. It might be in any event that my learned friend Mr. Re is concerned with at least a couple of those, so I should mention them. We've got some matters to raise about the witness Delalic, some matters to raise about -- look, I'm raise them after the witness, if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if those matters will take some time and we might sit in the afternoon for an hour to discuss it. It depends on how long this witness will take.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I stop talking, that will assist the witness. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We could also move quicker if we could get a list of issues that are to be raised so we can prepare for them and have the right personnel here for the matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think that's appropriate, Your Honours. So if -- if while this witness starts if I could just be temporarily excused from the court I'll go and get that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you're not going to do the cross-examination, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good. So we can have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I can promise you that we'll let you go today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good morning, I am Guenael Mettraux and I'm appearing on behalf Mr. Sefer Halilovic. Yesterday, in your evidence you gave a detailed account of your activities in the early hours of the 14th of September, 1993. Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sleeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm going to take you back at the time when you woke up, and I would like to go into private session to do that, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Madam, I'm taking you back to the first time when you went out. You've indicated that none of the bullets hit you at that stage. Did you see where the bullet landed? Was it on your house behind you, in the windows of your house behind you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because there was wind falling all over me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Sand falling all over me.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very well. Then you went back inside the house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And as far as you could tell, none of the soldiers tried to follow you in the house as you went to your house at that stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: You've begin evidence yesterday that as you were back inside your house you saw the soldiers setting fire to the barn in front of your house. Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That because you wanted to extinguish that fire, you decided to get out of your house again and confront the soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no intention of putting up resistance. All I wanted to do was put the fire out in the barn.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. My question was probably not very well put. What I meant to say is: You wanted to get out to extinguish the fire, and you decided and did so as a matter of fact despite the fact that those five individuals had shot at you a moment before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And when you went out again, madam, how far were you from the five soldiers in metres, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: 20 to 30 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you've indicated, I believe, that the soldiers started shooting at you again; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once I was out of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did the five soldiers shoot at you or was it one, two, three of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And did he fire single shots or was it a burst of fire again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a burst.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And none of the bullets hit you on that occasion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was when I came back into the house and went as far as the back door.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It was inside the house between the first and the second time when you came out again; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the first and second time, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I'd like now to ask you a few questions about the general situation in the village and in the area at the time. Please, I remind you not to mention the name of your village, and I will try to do the same as well. Would you agree that because the front line and enemy forces were close by, living in the villages around Uzdol was rather dangerous for civilians and soldiers; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: However, a number of people were attached to their homes, just like yourself, and decided to stay in the village despite the risk; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: However, to protect both the villages and villagers and soldiers who lived there, a number of measures were taken to protect both the villages and the people living in there, and the first such measures was a number of HVO positions, is that correct, in and around the villages?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: She can't answer as to the HVO strategy, the HVO decisions as to what to protect. It should be to a soldier or someone from the HVO command to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that the Defence counsel was not going to ask the strategy of the HVO, just from her own experience, whether she notice the any deployment of the HVO soldiers. Maybe, Mr. Mettraux, you could be more specific in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Madam, while you were living in the village in the month of August and September of 1993, did you observe any HVO positions in or near the village in which you lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it from the village, but I didn't go as far as the lines to have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: From your own observation, madam, and keep it -- keep it to that, how many of those outposts or HVO positions did you observe in or around the village in which you lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: All you could see from our village was a single position.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Was it a position which was inside the village or a position that was outside of the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And how far was it, madam, from your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And did you observe any other HVO positions as you would walk from your own village to other villages or, for example, to Cer? Did you see any other HVO positions during those walks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: During that period of August and September 1993, you didn't say at all time in your home, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So you walked around your village, and you also went on a number of occasion - I will come back to that - but you also went on a number of occasion to the village of Cer for instance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Well, what I'm trying to ask you is whether during those walks or during your going to the village of Cer you saw any HVO positions, other than the one which you've already mentioned to us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very well. Did you see or did you observe on -- either from your village or during those walks HVO positions, artillery positions? Did you observe any of those or is it something you didn't see at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: You saw, however, the tank which was placed next to the school in Cer, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was placed outside the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'd like to go back for a moment into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Madam, you've discussed also in your evidence-in-chief yesterday with the Prosecution an organisation known as the Home Guard. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, it may be a matter of terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we may have to go back for a second into private session. I'm sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go back to the closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Madam, this -- this group which you referred to as Domobrani, a home guards, was part of the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Are you able to say in approximate numbers how many people around Uzdol were members of Domobrani, Home Guard, even in general terms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unable to say the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: An approximate number will do if you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: About ten of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very well. And those individuals had been issued automatic weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But they carried weapons with them, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had M-48 rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Court, madam, could you tell us what an M-48 rifle is? Is that an older sort of rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm unable to explain that to you. I know that they called them M-48s.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that an automatic rifle or a semi-automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can we go back into private session, Your Honour, for a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Madam, you've indicated that a number of members of the Domobrani were living in other villages. Were any of them living in the village of Kriz?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And who was the person or the persons who were members of Domobrani and who lived in Kriz in September of 1993? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remember Ivan Ratkic from Kriz.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the witness please be shown what is now marked as -- it's an exhibit, D350.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: You're going to be shown another picture, madam, from the village of Kriz, and I'm going to ask you to make one short marking on that picture. Very well. Can you recognise the village, madam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can you locate on that picture the house where Ivan Ratkic was living in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can you please mark it with an H.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objection? Yes. It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Defence Exhibit 372.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Madam, is that correct that your father kept a hunting rifle at home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did he also keep any hand-grenades as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No, you don't know; or no, he didn't have any such weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he never brought any home.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you know him to have possessed any or carried any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was issued with any while standing guard, but he never brought any home.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know where was rifle was on the morning of the 14th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was under the sofa.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did you see the weapon that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did you go and look for it at any stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And at that time, madam, do you know where your brother was? Was he in the house, outside of the house? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very well. I think you've given some evidence yesterday about individuals involved in helping out with the army other than in combat duties or guard assignments, and I think you've given us some evidence that a number of women from the villages would go and cook for the soldiers in Cer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. They went there to clean and also to do the dishes and to wash. There were -- the chefs were there, the main cooks who normally worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And how often did you go to the school yourself during the month of August and September 1993? How regularly, if you want? Was it every day, once a week, twice a week?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in September 1993, madam, the school in Cer was the battalion command of the 3rd Corps of the Rama Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And during that period that is in the early days or weeks of September 1993 there were quite a large number of soldiers within the school at all times; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that, Your Honour. Quite a large number? This is an issue that there should be some numbers specifically stated. Quite a large number, we can be talking about thousands. What are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it was a general question, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe you could be more specific in this aspect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, madam, can you remember generally how many soldiers would be in the school at the time when you personally went there? Can you remember a number, an approximate number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never saw a large number of soldiers. There would always be between 10 and 15 soldiers when we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And are you aware at that time that there would be more or less than that and there was actually shifts of soldiers coming and going to the school? Is that something that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have no idea. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's okay. I would like now to take you to the last area of your evidence, and we will be done within five to ten minutes. In your evidence-in-chief yesterday, you described how you fled from your village and ran towards the village of Rajici. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you gave evidence yesterday about some shooting in your direction coming from your right and your left and hearing the sounds of "Allahu Akbar." Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Are you able to assess the distance from yourself as you ran and the people who you believed to be shooting at you? Are you able to make that assessment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And yet you didn't see any of the shooters yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was just shot at from left and from right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: What about the sounds of "Allahu Akbar," madam, was it coming from the right or the left? At the time you were running, that is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was coming from the left, from the direction of Prskalo's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very well. And you've indicated that you didn't recognise any of the persons whom you believed to be shooting at you. You didn't see any -- you didn't see the uniforms that those people might have been wearing at the time if any; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And none of the shots hit you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And did you see where the bullet landed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't as I was running.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So you were terrified and just kept on running. Would it be fair to say that you were going through a state of extreme excitement at the time trying to save your life? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, is that the fact that you run away in fear for your life and that you came across a soldier which you grabbed and it took you a few seconds to recognise that that man was in fact your uncle? And please don't mention his name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was the one who grabbed him because I was about to fall down. I could no longer stand on my own feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But as you grabbed your uncle, you didn't realise for a few seconds that he indeed was your uncle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not until he spoke and told me to run.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is it also correct that the man who was running behind you and whom you believed to be a Muslim soldier was in fact the Croatian neighbour of your uncle? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you very much, madam, for your patience. That would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As you were running after Rajici, or through Rajici, did you see any HVO soldiers arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was when we were on our way to Kranjcici that we saw lorries arriving from Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did those HVO soldiers shoot at you?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: The answer being questioned, but I'm struggling to see how it came out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, he is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness has already answered the question. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were asked about certain HVO soldiers that lived in your village. Do you know if any of those persons slept there on the evening of the 13th into the morning of the 14th? Were any of those persons present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were asked about civilians living in your village. Were civilians living in the village of Rajici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were civilians living in the village of Cer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were civilians living in the village of Kriz?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And civilians were living in the village of Zelenike?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You mentioned certain members of the Home Guard. Do you know if any of those persons were present on the eve -- during the sleeping hours of September 13th or the morning hours of September 14th? Were they present in their homes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about -- at the beginning of cross-examination about the uniforms that the soldiers were wearing, the camouflage uniforms, and you indicated that -- and also that all uniforms are the same. Had you ever heard any HVO soldiers ever yelling the chant "Allahu Akbar."

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't see how the witness could answer that question considering that she didn't know or she didn't give evidence as to who she saw or heard shouting "Allahu Akbar." This is pure assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, they have raised an issue this morning that all soldiers were wearing similar uniforms, and they're trying apparently to raise the inference that maybe their own soldiers were shooting at them. As a result, we have the right, Your Honour, to get into that issue, whether or not the HVO soldiers that she knows from the village or the HVO soldiers that she has seen ever used that chant, the same chant she heard that morning. Based on the inference they raised, Your Honour, we have the right on redirect examination to ask that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe this question is too obvious to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Then can she at least --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you could -- maybe you could put your question in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Of the HVO soldiers that you knew in your village and in the Uzdol area, had you ever heard them yell "Allahu Akbar" in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage are there any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No. I believe that all of ours are in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All have been tendered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Witness, thank you very much indeed for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. When we break, Madam Usher will show you out of the courtroom. We all wish you a very, very pleasant jury back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we only have about eight minutes left, so I don't think we have enough time to deal with those matters and the -- and I believe we have to resume at 2.15, and it will not last very long. So the hearing is adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 11.51 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. This is a continuation of this morning's proceedings. And in the morning we don't have time to deal with the procedural matters, but now I believe we have too much time to deal with it. Mr. Morrissey made a submission this morning and I believe that we'll give the floor to Mr. Morrissey first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour. There's four issues that can be dealt with. They may be really fact-finding episodes now. First of all, the issue of the Karic deposition. The Prosecution are considering their position about that. I presume that at some stage they'll submit a response. But two issues have to be determined about that. The first is: When should that deposition be played to the Court. And the next is that: Should the Tribunal rule in the Defence's favour and allow some limited further cross-examination of this man. Have steps been taken to put that into place? Now, as to the issue of when to play that deposition, it seemed to me that next week may be an opportunity to do that, because if we finish Mr. Karavelic within time, which we will do, of course, we may then have time for the pathologist, if the Prosecution are able to get the pathologist there, and of course that's their management issue; I'm not interfering with it. We may find ourselves with a bit of time next week and it may be then that it's appropriate to play the Karic deposition at that time. I raise it now as a possibility. I don't insist on it, but it may be a useful time to do it. What I do ask is the video -- that steps be taken to make a videolink available for Mr. Karic so in case Your Honours rule in favour of the Defence, that can be done. We don't know what his medical condition is. We've indicated a motion that the Defence team took the step of speaking to him to see whether he was -- with it, frankly to see whether he was able to talk and give sensible evidence. We're not doctors, but we formed the view that it is worth persisting with this request, and we do persist with it. That's why we saw him. But I can't give any medical opinion about him. Whatever his situation may be, the deposition was taken in case he took a turn for the worse and wasn't around. Therefore, speed is of the essence. In my submission, that ought to be booked straightaway. If Your Honours rule against us, it can be debooked. But we don't want a situation to develop where the Prosecution give you a good outline of argument; you then consider the situation and you then decide in your favour; and then we have to wait weeks after that. So it should be done immediately, in my submission. AnLed really, that's the first thing I want to raise about Karic. But I can go through all of my matters, but it's a matter for the Court whether they want to here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, let's deal with those items one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As to the Ramiz Delalic issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we should hear the response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll deal with those matters one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any response from the Prosecution or anything new that the Prosecution would like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is a response, Your Honour. We have a microphone not working at the back here, so I apologise if you can't all see me when I'm addressing you. The Prosecution -- we have of course received the additional -- the supplementary submissions regarding Mr. Karic's depositions. We will of course -- we will respond to this fairly promptly. I think we received it yesterday or on Wednesday afternoon. The -- much of it of course merely repeats the arguments which learned counsel, Mr. Morrissey, made when we argued -- when this was argued I think last week. When we argued it last week, our response was that if the depositions, if the Trial Chamber admits them, do not need to be played. There's no -- it's not a matter which the Trial Chamber needs to play as such in court time. I raise the precedent of the Simic case in which the Trial Chamber just admitted them into evidence, not even as an exhibit, but admitted them in and admitted the transcript. Because it's sworn evidence so it just becomes part of the trial proceedings. And then in the Simic judgement they refer at various parts to the trial transcript and at various parts to the deposition, Rule 71 transcript, which of course has a different page numbering. So in the Prosecution's submission, there's no need at all to even consider playing them in valuable court time. If the Trial Chamber wishes to view them, the Trial Chamber, in our submission, can do so. Of course it's a matter for Your Honours, but it would be a much better use of trial time, in our respectful submission, to do so out of court, and there's not anything on them Your Honours can't glean from reading them. So your first submission or response is: If they're admitted they should be admitted and become part of the trial record. In relation to the videolink, of course we support the application. We've already made our position clear that in Mr. Karic -- and we have contacted him and the Defence motion says so. He considers himself fit, according to our information, to give evidence, although reluctantly, via videolink. If the Trial Chamber rules that further evidence should be taken from him -- and I note in their supplementary submissions the Defence have referred to the fact that he is not on our witness list, but that is of no relevance, we submit, because it's a deposition. He's not a witness; it's a deposition evidence taken before. So our submission is if you accede to that request, yes of course the videolink should be booked, and as soon as possible, and obviously in those two weeks in May in which the trial would sit. Of course, that's a matter for the Trial Chamber. I think those are the only two issues Mr. Morrissey raised, unless there's another issue you want to me to respond on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I have a question for you, Mr. Re. Are you going to submit to us a written submission or are we going to take your oral submission as it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In response to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- this? Your Honours excuse me for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's really a matter of resources at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yeah, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We prefer to do it orally, but the Defence has raised some issues about the admissibility of some of the exhibits which were -- which were "tendered" or attempted to be tendered in the deposition hearing. That's not a matter I can deal with on the spot now. If Your Honours admit the deposition in, subject to further examination or not, it may be appropriate to hear oral argument on the admissibility of each of the -- there's not many, maybe half a dozen exhibits which were put forward at the time. The submission only says it in a blanket fashion, submits they shouldn't go it. In our submission, it's something that should be argued exhibit by exhibit, and the appropriate time would be when the Trial Chamber makes its decision. The deposition is one thing; the exhibits that are put to the witness during the deposition are another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you mean that you are going do respond in written form?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We'd prefer not to. I'm suggesting if we could do it orally at the time when Your Honours rule on it and the Defence could orally respond exhibit by exhibit, as you do with any other exhibits in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. Well, on this matter I believe that we are not in the position to make the ruling now, however we realise that it becomes a bit of an urgent matter. And we'll take into consideration of the submissions of both parties of this very issue, and we'll give our oral decision on this matter next week. And as for the videolink arrangements, I'm afraid that we couldn't do anything before any rulings on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. There is just one matter I have to add now. My learned friend raised the issue of whether you should play the deposition in open court. I believe you have to play it in open court. There's no basis for not doing it. In any event, if you have any discretion about that, I would be submitting that of course you would have to look at it and see it. This is a public trial in a public place. No protective measures are being sought by that witness. And really you'll be faced with a bit of a choice between the evidence of -- well a number of witnesses including Mr. Karic on one hand and the evidence of Witness D on the other. Your Honours may remember Witness D, I don't know if you do. But I would be very much concerned that you have the chance to see Mr. Karic and see him, and then remember Witness D, and see him, because that will help you to decide which one you accept. So wbles you do need to see that person giving his evidence and that's an important matter. Your Honours I'll move --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I just very briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In relation to that, could the record please reflect that the depositions were actually taken in open session. They were publicly taken. They were not taken in private session before Ms. Featherstone, the presiding officer. So they had been taken publicly played during the proceedings. I think they went for some three days. So you have to bear in mind that it's three days of court time to watch them again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, whether we have to play that deposition or not in the courtroom, I believe that we have to rely on the Rules of Procedure as well as the past practice of this Tribunal. And we'll deal with this matter all together in our ruling on this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As it is Tribunal pleases. Now, I move on to the next matter and that concerns Ramiz Delalic and I just ask that we go into the private session on this matter, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes -- oh, sorry, pardon me. Well, Your Honours, the time has come for the Prosecutors to tell us through which witness, if any, and when the Prosecution are proposing to lead this piece of evidence. And it's now also a scheduling matter for us to determine and for you, the Tribunal, also to determine when you would like to hear argument on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I believe the last time the OTP promised me that they would file something in this aspect in written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not sure we promised to file something. I thought we were to report back or at the end of the week to inform the Trial Chamber as to what our plans were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, are you in the position to inform us about your plan?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We intend, as I notified the Trial Chamber I think it was earlier this week, to attempt to tender the statement into evidence during the next suitable break of the proceedings, next week after Mr. Karavelic evidence, would from the Prosecution's view, be a suitable time to argue the point, subject of course to the convenience of the Trial Chamber. We don't plan to call the witness to tender it. Our witness will be in the argument that consistent with Tribunal jurisprudence. A statement - I specifically refer to the Kvocka case - a statement made to the Office of the Prosecutor ostensibly in accordance with the Rules is a prime facie admissible document. And if the Defence wish to challenge it, they are certainly entitled to do so. And once the Trial Chamber is satisfied prime facie it is an admissible document taken in accordance with the Rules, the Defence has a burden of persuasion to persuade the Trial Chamber that it should not be admitted. And what the Defence seem to have submitted, in our submission they would have to call some evidence on the point, from either Mr. Balijagic, former counsel, or the accused Mr. Halilovic himself. Because the suggestion appears to be - and it's only been made in a motion, not orally, and certainly before the trial, as it should hvae been - that Mr. Halilovic was "induced" by something that his counsel said to him. Now, if that's the situation, it's incumbent upon the Defence to call counsel for Mr. Halilovic to explain the circumstances of why he made a statement to the OTP in the presence of his lawyer, in accordance with the Rules, during which he was cautioned and advised of his rights on a number of occasions over the period in which the interview was conducted. So our submission is it that we are prepared to argue the matter properly. We haven't received a motion from the Defence about the tendering of record of interview or the statement, and we will do that at the next convenient moment for the Trial Chamber, and we suggest probably at the end of Mr. Karavelic's evidence to give the Defence time to put on their motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, on the following occasions there have been letters to the Prosecution asking what they propose to do now, 7th of February, 20th of February, 27th of February, 11th of March, 30th of March. Now, the Prosecutor here is plainly and clearly playing games and playing the clock. Now that we've got an indication from them that they are not proposing to call a witness or to lead it through a witness but are proposing to seek that it be tendered without any such testing, the Defence will in fact move a motion saying that we object to that being done. We will do so in writing. Now, we'll indicate that there's the possibility of calling evidence. My friend has mentioned two people. There could be two more. First of all, the investigator Nikolai Mikhailov, we received a letter from him saying that he refused to meet with the Defence. So an issue does not arise about him. The other one is Madame del Ponte, with respect to whom there were discussions then-counsel Mr. Balijagic concerning this interview and she may be a witness who is called. Now, if learned friend wishes to mention that there be some burden on the Defence, he has to remember this: The onus is on the Prosecution to prove voluntariness. If they don't want to call evidence, they're doomed. So it's a matter for the Prosecutor to determine what he wants to do and they want to do generally. Frankly, there may be evidence called here and if there is, we'll need to set aside some time for it. That's why at the start of this I said we need to work out the schedule. Now, that's a matter that I'm in the Tribunal's hands about. We'll meet the convenience of the Tribunal about that. And I think at the end of the evidence of Mr. Karavelic there might not be a lot of time, certainly not enough time to hear all the evidence that might be called. But it may be if no one calls any evidence, we would have time to put the arguments. I indicate now that since the Prosecution has been good enough to respond and tell us what his proposed times are, we're going to file a motion objecting to it. That's where the matter now stands. We'll file that. The Prosecution can respond. The question of whether parties want to call evidence or not can be dealt with in a proper way at that way. So could I ask now that the Court give some thought, the Tribunal give some thought to when that should take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage I believe that we have to read your submissions in written forms because we also have some problems with this kind of practice, as I mentioned before. According to our Rules there are several ways to admit documents into the evidence. That may be the live witness, we hear him, and through him we admit that document; the other way is the 92 bis, 94, the judicial notice, as well as 89 (C) and (F), which is within the discretion of this Bench. But this statement is different with others; this is the accused's himself interview. So we decided to approach it in a very careful way and do not be hasty to jump to conclusions at this stage. And the Prosecution is also welcome to submit a response on this issue so that we could be in a better position to assess the situation and to make our ruling. Anyway, since the Prosecution case is approaching to the end, I hope both parties will make the best use of the time available and submit to the Chamber as early as possible any comments, views, and response in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That will be done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution will most certainly do that. There are two things I just wish to briefly raise. The first is: My learned colleague, Mr. Morrissey, accused the Prosecution of "playing games" and playing the clock. Now, I don't want to get into sniping here; this is unnecessary. We are not playing games. The interview has always been on our exhibit list and we have never had a witness there you could logically link the tender of interview evidence through. It is clear that we have always intended to tender at some point, in the same was as records of interview in other cases interviews have been tendered, such as the Omarska and the Simic case. I was involved in both of those. They were both tendered from the bar table in those two cases. As an advance submission, I refer Your Honours -- and the Defence, of course -- to the Kvocka appeal judgement of the 28th of February, 2005, paragraphs 121 to 129, at which the very issue of tendering such at statement was discussed and an appeal against the tender was dismissed by the Appeals Chamber ruling, as Your Honour the Presiding Judge has just alluded to, that an interview with the accused falls into a very different category. At the moment I'm attempting to -- or attempting to ascertain the exact situation in every other trial here, but I suspect from my own experience that in most of them they've been tendered without a tendering witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. I think we'll do our own assessment at a later stage when we receive the filings from the parties. And of course both parties should regard the other party's activities in the face of the bona fide, unless there's preponderance of the evidence to show otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. Your Honour, the final matter that I would want to raise is the question of certain intercepts. We have flagged in the past an intention to oppose the admission into evidence of some intercepted telephone -- or some transcripts of telephone intercepts. And again, we want to make sure that the argument concerning those intercepts occurs at an appropriate time so that this is really a scheduling matter now. And although the Prosecution can say whatever they like, I'm not seeking to put them to their proof or to elicit an argument about it right now. But there are a couple of matters I would like to raise in connection with that. The first is we get an indication from the Prosecutor which witness is going to be the witness they wish to tender these transcripts through. I suspect that it may come to be Mr. Mujezinovic, but we just need that to be confirmed. Then we need to decide the timing of the argument in respect of that. We've got a motion that's half-drafted I suppose is the best way to put that. But we'll deal with that as soon as we can, as soon as it's appropriate to do it. We don't really want to just flood the Prosecution and the Chamber with motions all at once; it's not really fair to anyone, and therefore we just want to get an idea of when it's likely this matter would arise and when it would be appropriate to run the argument. So the Prosecutor might give us their thoughts about it and we can decide when it would be. There is one matter that arises. After the time that I flagged that there would be argument about that, the Prosecutor -- well, perhaps, Your Honours, could we just move into the private session for a minute, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into private session. So you mean you shook the tree again and something fell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what fell on our heads this time was a CD with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I thought we were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, my learned friend Mr. Mettraux has a number of other shorter matters today which today is probably a good time to raise those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, I will be very, very short, indeed. The other two matters which we would like to add at that stage. The first one is a tape played in the course of this week. This is Exhibit P312. You will remember on the document that was tendered, the CD which was tendered by the Prosecution, a part of the tape was actually missing. And we would like at the least the support of the Trial Chamber to put a request to CLSS for the transcript of the -- the transcript tendered by the Prosecution to be very fat, as we have spotted a number of problems, including the missing part that we've identified in court. We simply would like the support of the Trial Chamber in that regard, as we have encountered a number of difficulties with CLSS. Not that we should blame them for anything, but they have quite an extensive list of outstanding matters to deal with. But if that could be given some sort of priority, we would be grateful. The second matter which we wanted to bring to the attention of the Trial Chamber is simply to flag this issue for the Trial Chamber. My colleague Mr. Morrissey has mentioned a number of them, but there is a number of outstanding letters which we've sent to the Prosecution in the past few months and weeks and we are having some difficulties receiving answers in relation to some of those matters. And as I mentioned earlier, we will have some further discussions at some stage, but we would like to indicate at this stage that rather than filing motions after motions, which we also consider is unnecessary, those matters can be dealt with outside of court. But we have encountered some difficulties in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As for the matter concerning of the CLSS, I believe that we'll entrust the registrar to inform them to make our request as the priority one. But I cannot guarantee. I will do my best to help both parties concerning all those matters. It is a very good practice for the parties to meet together to discuss the matters and try to solve it out of the courtroom. I think only if there's some major problem that they could not solve out of court should those matters be brought to the attention of the Bench, and the Bench will do its best to help to solve this problem. Yes. As for next week's schedule, we have already said that at least we have two witnesses on our list. We might have extra sittings and try to finish the third one, but at this moment I could not guarantee that. The parties will be informed at the beginning of the next week, maybe Monday, to see whether if we could have extra sittings. Because of the e-court system because there are so many cases going on simultaneously, there are some difficulties, but we'll do our best to finish as many witnesses as possible. This is what I would say at this stage. Well, I think that's all for today's hearing, and we wish everybody a happy weekend. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 18th day of April, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.01 p.m.,
